title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps
subtitle: One unambiguous way to write a date and time, from 1985-04-12T23:20:50.52Z to a leap second.
summary: RFC 3339 defines the Internet Date/Time Format, a strict profile of ISO 8601 for writing a timestamp as text, such as 1996-12-19T16:39:57-08:00. It uses a four-digit year, most-significant field first, a fixed set of separators and a mandatory offset from UTC, so timestamps are unambiguous and sort correctly as plain strings. It is the date format used by many Internet protocols and data formats, including JSON APIs, Atom feeds and log files.

eli5.summary: People write dates all kinds of ways, so "10/11" can mean two different days. This RFC picks one recipe, year first, then month, then day, then time, and says what time zone you mean, so everybody reads the same moment.

tldr.problem: Dates like 10/11/1996, two-digit years and local times with no zone are read differently by different people and programs.
tldr.mechanism: A profile of ISO 8601 with one shape, YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS with optional fractional seconds and a required Z or numeric offset, where almost every field and separator is mandatory.
tldr.outcome: Timestamps are unambiguous, machine-parseable and sortable as strings, which is why so many protocols and APIs adopted the format.

today: RFC 3339 timestamps are everywhere. JSON APIs, Atom feeds, many log formats, OpenAPI and JSON Schema's date-time format, and the date handling in many programming languages and databases read and write this form. People often call such strings "ISO 8601" even though RFC 3339 is a narrower profile. RFC 9557 updates it with an optional suffix that carries a time zone name alongside the offset.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The authors open bluntly: "Date and time formats cause a lot of confusion and interoperability problems on the Internet." The RFC responds with an Internet profile of ISO 8601, which describes dates and times in the Gregorian calendar.

It deliberately covers only one use: timestamps for protocol events. That narrow scope has consequences the RFC lists. All dates are in the "current era", years 0000 to 9999. Every time has a stated relationship (an offset) to Coordinated Universal Time. A timestamp marks an instant, not a period, so durations and intervals are out of scope. And the format steers clear of scheduling questions such as what daylight saving time will do in the future, because the UTC time for "17:00 on 23rd March 2005 in New York" can depend on administrative decisions.

The specification is a timestamp format, not a calendar or scheduling format. It records when something happened, not when a meeting will happen.
sections.eli5: Everybody writes the date differently. Some start with the month, some with the day. This paper picks one way, only for saying exactly when something happened, so nobody gets mixed up.

sections.title: Definitions and Two-Digit Years
sections.content:
Section 2 defines the vocabulary: UTC as maintained by the BIPM, the second as 9,192,631,770 cycles of the cesium-133 hyperfine transition, a minute as 60 seconds, an hour as 60 minutes and a day as 24 hours. A leap year is divisible by four, except a centennial year must also be divisible by 400. "Z" is the suffix for a UTC offset of 00:00, often spoken "Zulu".

Section 3 deals with the Y2K-era problem of two-digit years. Internet protocols MUST generate four-digit years. Two-digit years are deprecated and, if received, should be accepted only when a wrong guess will not cause a protocol or processing failure, such as when they are only used for logging. The RFC even describes broken programs that print the year 2000 as 100 (year minus 1900) or as :0 (adding the decade to the ASCII character zero) and says robust parsers may detect them.
sections.eli5: Saying "the year 02" is confusing, because it could be 1902 or 2002. So always write all four digits.

sections.title: UTC, Offsets and Local Time
sections.content:
Because daylight saving rules are "so convoluted" and change with local law, the RFC says true interoperability is best achieved by using UTC. When a local time is useful, it is given with a numeric offset calculated as "local time minus UTC". To convert, subtract the offset: 18:50:00-04:00 is the same instant as 22:50:00Z.

Alphabetic zone names like "EST" caused poor interoperability in the past, so only numeric offsets are allowed. Offsets are whole minutes, as in ISO 8601, so some historical zones can only be approximated.

Section 4.3 gives a special case. If the UTC time is known but the local offset is not, write the offset as -00:00. That differs in meaning from Z or +00:00, which say UTC is the preferred reference.

Section 4.4 rejects unqualified local time, a time with no zone information. It would be misread across about 23/24 of the globe, so such systems must use NTP or another mechanism to get the correct UTC time.
sections.eli5: The time on your wall clock depends on where you live. So the paper says: also tell us how far your clock is from the world's main clock. If you don't know, put a special mark that says "I don't know".

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
Section 5 starts with qualities the authors want, and each one explains a choice in the final grammar.

Ordering
Fields run from least precise (year) to most precise (second), so timestamps in the same zone and with the same number of fractional digits sort correctly as plain strings.
Human readability, with balance
A date like 10/11/1996 is "completely unsuitable for global interchange". Clients should still convert to a display format suited to the user's locale.
No rarely used options
Rare options are rarely tested, so parsers break on them. The only one kept is fractional seconds.
No redundancy
A weekday name can disagree with the date, so it is left out; Appendix B shows how to compute it.
Simplicity
The full ISO 8601 grammar is too complex, so the profile makes most fields and punctuation mandatory.
sections.eli5: The rules are simple on purpose: biggest piece first, no pieces you can leave out, and nothing that could say two different things at once.

sections.title: The Internet Date/Time Format
sections.content:
Section 5.6 gives the grammar in ABNF. A date-time is a full-date, the letter "T", then a full-time. The full date is a four-digit year, two-digit month and two-digit day, separated by hyphens. The full time is hours, minutes and seconds separated by colons, optionally followed by a fraction of a second (a dot and one or more digits), and then a mandatory offset: either Z or a sign with hours and minutes.

The RFC says this profile SHOULD be used in new Internet protocols. Per ABNF, the letters "T" and "Z" may also be lower case, but applications that generate the format SHOULD use upper case. A specification may also choose to separate date and time with a space for readability.

The five examples in section 5.8 range from 1985-04-12T23:20:50.52Z to 1937-01-01T12:00:27.87+00:20, the latter being the closest representable offset to Netherlands time, which was 19 minutes 32.13 seconds ahead of UTC.
sections.eli5: The recipe is: year, month, day, then the letter T, then hour, minute, second, and finally the time zone. It is like writing the biggest box first, then the smaller boxes inside it.

sections.title: Restrictions and Leap Seconds
sections.content:
The grammar allows values the calendar does not, so section 5.7 adds restrictions. The day number depends on month and year: 31 days in January, March, May, July, August, October and December; 30 in April, June, September and November; and 28 or 29 in February. Appendix C gives a C function for the leap-year test.

Seconds normally run 00 to 59, but the value 60 is allowed for an inserted leap second at the end of June or December, and a subtracted leap second would make the maximum 58. In time zones other than Z the leap second point shifts by the offset, so it still occurs at the same instant everywhere. For example, 1990-12-31T23:59:60Z and 1990-12-31T15:59:60-08:00 are the same instant.

Leap seconds cannot be predicted far ahead, so applications should not generate timestamps with inserted leap seconds until they are announced. The hour is limited to 00 through 23: ISO 8601 allows 24, but this profile does not, to reduce confusion.
sections.eli5: Most minutes have 60 seconds, but sometimes the world's clock-keepers add one extra second, number 60, to match the slowing Earth. The rules say when that is allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Appendices
sections.content:
The security section is brief. A site's local time zone may reveal when systems are least likely to be watched, which could help someone pick a time for a security probe, so some sites may prefer to emit times in UTC only. The RFC adds that others may regard this as "loss of useful functionality at the hands of paranoia".

The appendices are informational. Appendix A is an ABNF translation of the full ISO 8601 syntax, with a warning that it "may contain errors" and that ISO 8601 remains authoritative. Appendix B has sample C code, based on Zeller's Congruence, to find the day of the week from a date. Appendix C has the leap-year function. Appendix D explains leap seconds: the International Earth Rotation Service decides them, with first preference given to the end of December and June, and second preference to the end of March and September.

The RFC is updated by RFC 9557, which adds an optional bracketed suffix for the time zone name and other information.
sections.eli5: Writing your local time zone can tell strangers when you are asleep. If that worries you, use the world's main clock instead. The back of the paper has extra helpers, like how to figure out which weekday a date falls on.

data.title: Timestamp layout (US-ASCII text, 8 bits per character)

fields.name: date-mday
fields.desc: Two digits, 01-31 depending on month and year.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Separates date from time (may be lower case t; generators SHOULD use upper case).

fields.name: time-second
fields.desc: Two digits, 00-59, or 60 for a leap second (58 if one is subtracted). An optional time-secfrac (a dot and 1 or more digits) may follow.

fields.name: Offset sign
fields.desc: + or - for time-numoffset (Z alone is used for UTC).

data.title: Internet Date/Time grammar
data.code:
date-fullyear   = 4DIGIT
date-month      = 2DIGIT  ; 01-12
date-mday       = 2DIGIT  ; 01-28, 01-29, 01-30, 01-31
time-hour       = 2DIGIT  ; 00-23
time-minute     = 2DIGIT  ; 00-59
time-second     = 2DIGIT  ; 00-58, 00-59, 00-60
time-secfrac    = "." 1*DIGIT
time-numoffset  = ("+" / "-") time-hour ":" time-minute
time-offset     = "Z" / time-numoffset

partial-time    = time-hour ":" time-minute ":" time-second
                  [time-secfrac]
full-date       = date-fullyear "-" date-month "-" date-mday
full-time       = partial-time time-offset

date-time       = full-date "T" full-time

viz.caption: WHAT THE PROFILE DROPS FROM ISO 8601

items.title: Basic format
items.text: Only the extended form with hyphens and colons is used, never 19961219T163957.

items.title: Week and ordinal dates
items.text: Only calendar dates (year, month, day), not week numbers or day-of-year.

items.title: Hour 24 and partial forms
items.text: Hours are 00 to 23, and no field may be left out.

items.title: Durations and periods
items.text: Intervals such as P1Y2M or start/end pairs are out of scope; a timestamp is one instant.
